  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}
  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,
  1130	  \end{equation*}
  1131	  where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $u$ from $V$.
  1132	\end{lemma}
  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:
  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}
  1137	  \omega^{\tr(a(b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;,
  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.
  1140	
  1141	For systems with many qudits, we will consider tensor products of the operators
  1142	$\qp^W$.
  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by
  1144	$\qp^W(a)$ the tensor product $\qp^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \qp^W(a_n)$.
  1145	These obey the twisted commutation relations
  1146	\begin{equation*}
  1147	  \forall a,b\in \Fq^n,\qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) \,=\, \omega^{-\tr (a \cdot
  1148	    b)}\, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;,
  1149	\end{equation*}
  1150	where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \in \Fq$.
  1151	For $W\in\{X,Z\}$ and $e \in \Fq^n$ define the eigenstates
  1152	\[ \ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}\;, \]
  1153	and associated rank-$1$ projectors $\qp^W_e$. Analogous versions of \Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1154	and \Cref{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single} relate the multi-qubit observables
  1155	and projectors:
  1156	\begin{align}
  1157	  \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b \in \Fq^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}
  1158	  \qp^W_b\;, \label{eq:pauli-obs-proj} \\
  1159	    \E_{a\in \F_q^n} \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)} \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b'\in \F_q^n} \E_{a\in \F_q^n}
  1160	  \omega^{\tr(a\cdot (b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;. \label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
  1161	\end{align}
  1162	
  1163	Since we only consider finite fields $\F_q$ such that $q = 2^k$ the maximally
  1164	entangled state $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and the corresponding qudit Pauli
  1165	observables/projectors are isomorphic to a tensor product of maximally entangled
  1166	states $\ket{\EPR_2}$ and \emph{qubit} Pauli observables/projectors
  1167	respectively; this is shown in the next lemma.
  1168	This is used to argue that the Pauli basis test (described in
  1169	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) gives a self-test for Pauli observables and
  1170	maximally entangled states over qubits.

   323		An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form

   325			f(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m}
   326			c_\alpha\, x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   327		\]
   328		with coefficients $c_\alpha \in \F_q$; the coefficients are uniquely
   329		determined by $f$, since the $q^m$ monomial functions indexed by
   330		$\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m$ span the $q^m$-dimensional space of all
   430		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   431	\end{definition}

   433	\section{Lines}
   434	
   435	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   436	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   437	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   438	
   439	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   440		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   441		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   442		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   443			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   444		\end{equation}
   445		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   446		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   447		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   448		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   449		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   450		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   451		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   452		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   453	\end{definition}
   454	
   455	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   456		\uses{def:line}
   457		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   458		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   459	\end{proposition}
   460	\begin{proof}
   461		\uses{def:line}
   462		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   463		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   464		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   465		inclusion.
   466	\end{proof}
   467	
   468	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   469	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   470	representation is obtained as follows.
   471	
   472	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   473		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   474		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   475		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   476		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   477		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   478		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   479		\[
   480			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   481		\]
   482		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   483		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   484		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   485		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   486		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   487		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   488		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   489		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   490		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   491		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   492	\end{definition}

   525	\section{Generalized Pauli observables}

   529	\begin{definition}[Generalized Pauli observables]\label{def:generalized-pauli}
   530		\uses{def:subfield-trace, def:lin-reg}
   531		Let $p$ be a prime and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$. The \emph{generalized Pauli
   532		observables over $\F_p$} are the unitaries on $\C^{\F_p}$ given by
   533		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-fp}
   534			\sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   535			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   536			\sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \omega^{bj} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   537		\end{equation}
   538		for $a, b \in \F_p$, with arithmetic over $\F_p$. For $q = p^k$, the
   539		\emph{generalized Pauli observables over $\F_q$} are the unitaries on
   540		$\C^{\F_q}$
   541		\[
   542			\tau^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   543			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   544			\tau^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \omega^{\tr(bj)} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   545		\]
   546		for $a, b \in \F_q$, where $\tr$ here denotes $\tr_{q \to p}$
   547		(Definition~\ref{def:subfield-trace}); for admissible $q$ this agrees with
   548		the standing shorthand, $p = 2$, and $\omega = -1$, so that all phases are
   549		signs. All the $\tau^X$ operators commute with one another, as do all the
   550		$\tau^Z$ operators. Their common eigenbases consist of the vectors
   551		$\ket{e_W}$, labeled by $e \in \F_q$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
   552		\[
   553			\ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{j \in \F_q}
   554			\omega^{-\tr(ej)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
   555			\ket{e_Z} = \ket{e}\;;
   556		\]
   557		the Fourier transform
   558		\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-f}
   559			F = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b \in \F_q}
   560			\omega^{-\tr(ab)} \ket{a}\bra{b}
   561		\end{equation}
   562		maps the computational ($Z$) eigenbasis to the $X$ eigenbasis. We write
   563		$\{\tau^W_e\}_{e \in \F_q}$ for the projective measurement whose elements
   564		are the rank-one projectors onto the vectors of the $W$ eigenbasis. For
   565		systems of $n$ qudits, we write, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a \in \F_q^n$,
   566		\[
   567			\tau^W(a) = \tau^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \tau^W(a_n)\;, \qquad
   568			\ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}
   569		\]
   570		for $e \in \F_q^n$, with associated rank-one projectors $\tau^W_e$.
   571	\end{definition}
   572	
   573	\begin{lemma}[Product and twisted commutation relations]\label{lem:twisted-commutation}
   574		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   575		Let $q = p^k$, let $n \ge 1$ be an integer, and let $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   576		\begin{enumerate}
   577			\item For all $a, a' \in \F_q$ and $b \in \F_p$,
   578			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
   579				      \tau^W(a)\, \tau^W(a') = \tau^W(a + a')
   580				      \qquad \text{and} \qquad
   581				      \bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^b = \tau^W(ab)\;;
   582			      \end{equation}
   583			      in particular $\bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^p = \Id$, so each
   584			      $\tau^W(a)$ is a unitary with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots
   585			      of unity.
   586			\item For all $a, b \in \F_q^n$,
   587			      % Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   588			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fq}
   589				      \tau^X(a)\, \tau^Z(b)
   590				      = \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^Z(b)\, \tau^X(a)\;,
   591			      \end{equation}
   592			      where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i \in \F_q$. The case
   593			      $q = p$, $n = 1$ reads
   594			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fp}
   595				      \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b)
   596				      = \omega^{-ab}\, \sigma^Z(b)\, \sigma^X(a)
   597				      \qquad \text{for all } a, b \in \F_p\;.
   598			      \end{equation}
   599		\end{enumerate}
   600	\end{lemma}
   601	\begin{proof}
   602		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   603		All identities are verified on computational basis states. For the product
   604		relations with $W = X$, shifting twice by $a'$ and $a$ equals shifting by
   605		$a + a'$; with $W = Z$, the phases $\omega^{\tr(aj)}\omega^{\tr(a'j)}$
   606		combine by $\F_q$-linearity of the trace, and the power relation follows by
   607		iterating. For the scalar twisted commutation,
   608		$\tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$, while
   609		$\tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(b(j+a))}\ket{j + a} =
   610		\omega^{\tr(ab)}\,\omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$. The multi-qudit relation
   611		follows by applying the scalar relation factor by factor and summing the
   612		exponents, using $\tr(a \cdot b) = \sum_i \tr(a_i b_i)$. For $q = p$ the
   613		trace is the identity map, which gives \eqref{eq:twisted-fp}.
   614	\end{proof}
   615	
   616	\begin{lemma}[Fourier cancellation over a subspace]\label{lem:cancellation}
   617		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal, def:subfield-trace}
   618		Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_q^k$ and let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$, where
   619		$p$ is the characteristic of $\F_q$ and $\tr = \tr_{q \to p}$. For all
   620		$v \notin V^\perp$,
   621		\[
   622			\E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr(\bu \cdot v)} = 0\;,
   623		\]
   624		where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $\bu$ in $V$.
   625	\end{lemma}
   626	\begin{proof}
   627		This is Fact 3.2 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Since $v \notin V^\perp$,
   628		the $\F_q$-linear functional $u \mapsto u \cdot v$ is not identically zero
   629		on $V$, hence surjective onto $\F_q$; composing with the nonzero map $\tr$
   630		shows that there is $u_0 \in V$ with $\tr(u_0 \cdot v) \neq 0$. Writing $C$
   631		for the expectation, translation invariance of the uniform distribution on
   632		$V$ gives
   633		$C = \E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr((\bu + u_0) \cdot v)}
   634		= \omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)}\, C$, and $\omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)} \neq 1$
   635		forces $C = 0$.
   636	\end{proof}

    47	\section{Games and strategies}

    51	\begin{definition}[Two-player one-round games]\label{def:game}
    52		A \emph{two-player one-round game} $\mathfrak G$ is specified by a tuple $(\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ where
    53		\begin{enumerate}
    54			\item $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ are finite sets, called the \emph{question alphabets},
    55			\item $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ are finite sets, called the \emph{answer alphabets},
    56			\item $\mu$ is a probability distribution over $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$, called the \emph{question distribution}, and
    57			\item $D \colon \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \times \mathcal A \times \mathcal B \to \{0,1\}$ is a function, called the \emph{decision predicate}.
    58		\end{enumerate}
    59	\end{definition}
    60	
    61	\begin{definition}[Tensor product strategies]\label{def:tensor-product-strategy}
    62		\uses{def:game, def:povm-conventions}
    63		A \emph{tensor product strategy} $\mathcal S$ for a game $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ is a tuple $(\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ where
    64		\begin{itemize}
    65			\item $\ket{\psi}$ is a pure quantum state, i.e.\ a unit vector in $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ for finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_A$, $\mathcal H_B$,
    66			\item $A$ is a set $\{A^x\}$ such that for every $x \in \mathcal X$, $A^x = \{A^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ is a POVM on $\mathcal H_A$, and
    67			\item $B$ is a set $\{B^y\}$ such that for every $y \in \mathcal Y$, $B^y = \{B^y_b\}_{b \in \mathcal B}$ is a POVM on $\mathcal H_B$.
    68		\end{itemize}
    69	\end{definition}
    70	
    71	\begin{definition}[Tensor product value]\label{def:tensor-product-value}
    72		\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy}
    73		The \emph{tensor product value} of a tensor product strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ with respect to a game $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ is
    74		\[
    75			\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) = \sum_{x,\,y,\,a,\,b} \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\, \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}\,.
    76		\]
    77		For $v \in [0,1]$ we say that the strategy $\mathcal S$ \emph{passes (or wins) $\mathfrak G$ with probability $v$} if $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) \ge v$. The \emph{tensor product value} of $\mathfrak G$ is
    78		\[
    79			\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G) = \sup_{\mathcal S} \operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S)\,,
    80		\]
    81		where the supremum is taken over all tensor product strategies $\mathcal S$ for $\mathfrak G$.
    82	\end{definition}
    83	
    84	Unless specified otherwise, all strategies considered in what follows are tensor product strategies, and we simply call them \emph{strategies}; similarly, we refer to $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ as the \emph{value} of the game $\mathfrak G$.
    85

    87	% by the low individual degree test track (Chapter 2), where it names the strategy format
    88	% specific to that test, so a distinct label is used here; see the following remark.
    89	\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]\label{def:projective-strategy-general}
    90		\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy, def:povm-conventions}
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[PCC and SPCC strategies]\label{def:spcc}
   167		\uses{def:projective-strategy-general, def:consistent-strategy, def:comm-strategy, def:symmetric-game}
   168		We say that a strategy $\mathcal S$ for a game $\mathfrak G$ is \emph{PCC} if it is projective, consistent, and commuting for $\mathfrak G$. Additionally, we say that a PCC strategy $\mathcal S$ is \emph{SPCC} if it is furthermore symmetric.

   171	\section{Distance measures}
   172	
   173	\begin{definition}[Distance between states]\label{def:state-distance}
   174		Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ be two families of states in the same space $\mathcal H$. For a function $\delta \colon \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted $\ket{\psi} \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if
   175		\[
   176			\lVert \ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n} \rVert^2 = O(\delta(n))\,.
   177		\]
   178		The dependence of the states and of $\delta$ on the indexing parameter $n$ is generally left implicit; we write, e.g., $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.
   179	\end{definition}
   180	
   181	\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]\label{def:consistency}
   182		\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
   183		Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ be POVMs. We write
   184		\[
   185			A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a
   186		\]
   187		on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
   188		\[
   189			\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi} = O(\delta)\,.
   190		\]
   191		In this case we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$. As in Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}, the $O(\cdot)$ refers to families of POVMs and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and is taken as $n \to \infty$.
   192	\end{definition}
   193	
   194	A measurement that is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same state under the singleton distribution, and vice versa: if $\sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = 1$, then $M_a \ot \Id\, \ket{\psi} = \Id \ot M_a\, \ket{\psi}$ for every $a$, by the equality case of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied outcome by outcome.
   195	
   196	% The source (references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:257-274) states this
   197	% definition for pairs of POVMs but applies the relation to arbitrary operator families:
   198	% to plain operators at 06:313-330, to sets of matrices at 06:364-380, and to products and
   199	% commutators, compared against the zero family, at 06:409-445. The general form below,
   200	% for arbitrary finite families of operators, is the one of the NEEXP source
   201	% (references/neexp-paper/05_quantum_preliminaries.tex:385-391), from which the distance
   202	% calculus is imported; the POVM case is singled out after the display.
   203	\begin{definition}[State-dependent distance between operator families]\label{def:povm-distance}
   204		\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
   205		Let $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal A$ be finite sets and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{M^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ and $\{N^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ be two families of linear operators on $\mathcal H$. We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   206		\[
   207			\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_a \lVert (M^x_a - N^x_a)\, \ket{\psi} \rVert^2 \le O(\delta)\,,
   208		\]
   209		and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state $\ket{\psi}$ and the distribution $\mu$ are clear from context. This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance. The principal case is that in which $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are POVMs on $\mathcal H$, and we then speak of the state-dependent distance between the POVMs; but the relation is used for arbitrary operator families --- for instance for products of measurement operators, or for commutators compared against the identically zero family, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:commutation-analysis} below.
   210	\end{definition}
   211	
   212	\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]\label{def:strategy-distance}
   213		\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy, def:state-distance, def:povm-distance}
   214		Let $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game and let $\mathcal S = (\psi, A, B)$ and $\mathcal S' = (\psi', A', B')$ be strategies for $\mathfrak G$. For $\delta \in [0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\mathcal S$ is $\delta$-close to $\mathcal S'$} if the following conditions hold.
   215		\begin{enumerate}
   216			\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same Hilbert space $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
   217			\item For all $x \in \mathcal X$ and $y \in \mathcal Y$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations holding under the distribution $\mu$ (i.e.\ under its corresponding marginals), on either $\ket{\psi}$ or $\ket{\psi'}$.
   218		\end{enumerate}
   219	\end{definition}

   221	\begin{remark}[Asymptotic reading of the distance relations]\label{rem:asymptotic-distance}

   441	\section{Conditionally linear functions and distributions}
   442	% Paper subsection label sec:cl kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   443	\label{sec:cl}
   444	
   445	Conditionally linear functions specify the question distributions of the games considered in the following chapters in a form that can be ``introspected''. Intuitively, a conditionally linear function takes as input an element $x \in V = \F^n$ and applies linear maps $L_j$ sequentially to $x^{V_j}$, where $V_1, V_2, \dots$ is a sequence of complementary register subspaces such that both the linear map $L_j$ and the subspace $V_j$, for $j \ge 2$, may depend on the values taken by the previous linear maps $L_1(x^{V_1})$, $L_2(x^{V_2})$, and so on.
   446	
   447	Throughout this section $V$ denotes the linear space $\F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$, and all the distinguished subspaces of $V$ are register subspaces (Definition~\ref{def:register-subspace}). If $V_1, V_2, \dots, V_\ell$ are fixed subspaces of $V$ and $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$, we use the subscript range notation
   448	\[
   449		V_{<k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,1 \le j < k} V_j\,, \qquad V_{>k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,\ell \ge j > k} V_j\,,
   450	\]
   451	and $V_{\le k}$, $V_{\ge k}$ are understood to be $V_{<k+1}$ and $V_{>k-1}$, respectively. For a register subspace $V'$ of $V$, the symbol $x^{V'}$ denotes the projection of $x$ onto $V'$ parallel to the complementary register subspace (Definition~\ref{def:complementary}). Moreover, if $F \colon V' \to V'$ is a function and $x \in V$, we write $x^F$ for $F(x^{V'})$; for example, in the following definition $x^{L_1}$ is shorthand for $L_1(x^{V_1})$.
   452	
   453	\begin{definition}[Conditionally linear functions]\label{def:cl-func}
   454		\uses{def:register-subspace, def:complementary}
   455		Let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some $n \ge 0$. For all integers $\ell \ge 0$ the collection of \emph{$\ell$-level conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is defined inductively as follows.
   456		\begin{enumerate}
   457			\item There is a single $0$-level conditionally linear function, which is the $0$ function on $V$.
   458			\item Let $\ell \ge 1$ and suppose the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear functions has been defined. The collection of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions on $V$ consists of all functions $L$ on $V$ that can be expressed in the following form: there exist complementary register subspaces $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ of $V$, a linear function $L_1$ on $V_1$, and, for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$, an $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear function $L_{>1,\,v}$ on $V_{>1}$, such that for all $x \in V$,
   459			\[
   460				L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})\,.
   461			\]
   462		\end{enumerate}
   463	\end{definition}
   464	
   465	We abbreviate ``conditionally linear'' as \emph{CL}. Operationally, an $\ell$-level CL function first applies $L_1$ to $x^{V_1}$; conditioned on the value $x^{L_1}$ it selects a register subspace $V_2$ and a linear map $L_2$ and applies $L_2$ to $x^{V_2}$; and so on, finally outputting $\sum_{k=1}^{\ell} x^{L_k}$. Every $1$-level CL function is linear, and conversely every linear map on $V$ is a $1$-level CL function. Moreover, for every $\ell \ge 1$ the collection of $\ell$-level CL functions contains the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level CL functions.
   466	
   467	\begin{definition}[Conditionally linear distributions]\label{def:cl-dist}
   468		\uses{def:cl-func}
   469		Let $L, R \colon V \to V$ be conditionally linear functions. The \emph{conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ corresponding to $(L,R)$} is the distribution over pairs $(L(x), R(x)) \in V \times V$ for $x$ drawn uniformly at random from $V$.
   470	\end{definition}
   471	
   472	Note that both players' questions are generated from the \emph{same} uniformly random seed $x$; this shared-seed structure is what the introspection technique exploits. The following lemma elucidates the structural properties of $\ell$-level CL functions. Recall that $x^{L_{<k}}$ and $x^{L_k}$ denote $L_{<k}(x)$ and $L_{k,\,u}(x^{V_{k,\,u}})$ where $u = L_{<k}(x)$.
   473	
   474	\begin{lemma}[Structure of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-kth}
   475		\uses{def:cl-func, def:register-subspace}
   476		Let $\ell \ge 1$ and $V = \F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$. A function $L \colon V \to V$ is an $\ell$-level CL function if and only if the following collection of functions and subspaces exists:
   477		\begin{enumerate}
   478			\item[(i)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$, a function $L_{\le k} \colon V \to V$, called the \emph{$k$-th marginal of $L$};
   479			\item[(ii)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{<k}(V)$, a register subspace $V_{k,\,u}$ of $V$, called the \emph{$k$-th factor space with prefix $u$};
   480			\item[(iii)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{<k}(V)$, a linear map $L_{k,\,u} \colon V_{k,\,u} \to V_{k,\,u}$, called the \emph{$k$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix $u$};
   481		\end{enumerate}
   482		such that the following conditions hold for all $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$:
   483		\begin{enumerate}
   484			\item $L_{\le k}$ is a $k$-level CL function on $V$;
   485			\item $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell} V_{i,\,x^{L_{<i}}}$ for all $x \in V$;
   486			\item $L_{\le k}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} x^{L_i}$ for all $x \in V$, where $L_i$ is shorthand notation for $L_{i,\,x^{L_{<i}}}$;
   487			\item $L = L_{\le \ell}$.
   488		\end{enumerate}
   489		As in condition 3, we sometimes use $V_k$ and $L_k$ to denote $V_{k,\,u}$ and $L_{k,\,u}$ respectively, leaving the prefix $u$ implicit.
   490	\end{lemma}
   491	\begin{proof}
   492		\uses{def:cl-func}
   493		For the ``if'' direction, conditions 1 and 4 immediately exhibit $L$ as an $\ell$-level CL function. For the ``only if'' direction one constructs the marginals, factor spaces, and linear maps by induction on $\ell$. In the base case $\ell = 1$ take $L_{\le 1} = L$, $V_1 = V$, and $L_1 = L$. For the inductive step, write $L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})$ as in Definition~\ref{def:cl-func} and apply the inductive hypothesis to each $(\ell-1)$-level function $L_{>1,\,v}$, obtaining its marginals, factor spaces, and linear maps over $V_{>1}$. Define $L_{\le 1} = L_1$ with first factor space $V_1$, and for $k \ge 2$ define $L_{\le k}(x) = x^{L_1} + L'_{x^{L_1},\,<k}(x^{V_{>1}})$, with the $k$-th factor space and linear map of $L$ with prefix $u$ given by those of $L_{>1,\,v}$ at index $k-1$ with prefix $w$, where $v = u^{V_1}$ and $w = u^{V_{>1}}$. Conditions 1--4 are then verified directly from the inductive hypothesis: the direct-sum decomposition of $V_{>1}$ extends to $V$ by adjoining $V_1$, and the sum formula for $L_{\le k}$ follows by unfolding the inductive marginals.
   494	\end{proof}
   495	
   496	The marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given CL function $L$ need not be unique. For example, the identity function on $V = \F^n$ is a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a $k$-level CL function for any $k \in \{2, \dots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition of $V$ into factor spaces.
   497	
   498	\begin{lemma}[Concatenation of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-concat}
   499		\uses{def:cl-func}
   500		Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and let $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces. Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and, for each $u \in L(U)$, $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL function on $V$. Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$, defined by
   501		\[
   502			T(x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)}(x^V)\,,
   503		\]
   504		is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U \oplus V$.
   505	\end{lemma}
   506	\begin{proof}
   507		\uses{def:cl-func}
   508		By induction on $k$. The case $k = 0$ follows directly from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, since then $L = 0$ and $T$ acts by the single $\ell$-level function $R_0$ on the register subspace $V$. For the inductive step, write $L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}})$ with complementary register subspaces $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$. For each value $x^{L_1}$, the function $T_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}$ on $U_{>1} \oplus V$ sending $x^{U_{>1} \oplus V}$ to $L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}) + R_{x^{L_1} + x^{L_{>1}}}(x^V)$ is the concatenation of the $(k-1)$-level function $L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}$ with a family drawn from $\{R_u\}$, hence is $(k+\ell-1)$-level by the induction hypothesis. The claim then follows from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func} applied with first subspace $U_1$ and first linear map $L_1$.
   509	\end{proof}
   510	
   511	% The source (references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364) leaves
   512	% the number m of summands unquantified (m >= 1 is needed for the level max_j ell_j to
   513	% have an index) and begins its induction at level 1; the level-zero base case is supplied
   514	% here, since def:cl-func admits 0-level functions and all ell_j may be 0.
   515	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-func-prod}
   516		\uses{def:cl-func, def:register-subspace}
   517		Let $m \ge 1$ be an integer and let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \dots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$. Suppose that, for each $j \in \{1, 2, \dots, m\}$, $L^{(j)}$ is an $\ell_j$-level conditionally linear function on $V^{(j)}$. Then the direct sum $L = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}$, defined by
   518		\[
   519			L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   520		\]
   521		for all $x = \sum_{j=1}^m x^{(j)} \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$, is an $\ell$-level CL function on $V$ for $\ell = \max_j \{\ell_j\}$; the maximum exists since $m \ge 1$.
   522	\end{lemma}
   523	\begin{proof}
   524		\uses{def:cl-func}
   525		Since an $\ell$-level CL function is also $k$-level conditionally linear for all $k \ge \ell$, it suffices to prove the claim when $\ell_j = \ell$ for all $j$. Proceed by induction on $\ell$. For $\ell = 0$ every $L^{(j)}$ is the zero function on $V^{(j)}$, so $L$ is the zero function on $V$, which is the unique $0$-level CL function on $V$ (Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}). For the inductive step with $\ell \ge 1$, decompose each $L^{(j)}$ into its first-level linear part $L^{(j)}_1$ on $V^{(j)}_1$ and its family of $(\ell-1)$-level remainders $L^{(j)}_{>1,\,v_j}$ on $V^{(j)}_{>1}$. The direct sums of the first-level parts define a linear map on $V_1 = \bigoplus_j V^{(j)}_1$, and, for each prefix value $v = \sum_j v_j$, the direct sums of the remainders are $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear on $V_{>1} = \bigoplus_j V^{(j)}_{>1}$ by the induction hypothesis. This exhibits $L$ in the form required by Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   526	\end{proof}
   527	
   528	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums give product distributions]\label{lem:cl-dist-prod}
   529		\uses{def:cl-dist, lem:cl-func-prod}
   530		For each $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ let $L^{(i)}, R^{(i)} \colon V^{(i)} \to V^{(i)}$ be $\ell_i$-level conditionally linear functions, and let $L, R \colon V \to V$ be the direct sums $L = \bigoplus_i L^{(i)}$ and $R = \bigoplus_i R^{(i)}$, as defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}. Then the conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ is the product distribution $\prod_{i=1}^m \mu_{L^{(i)},\,R^{(i)}}$ over $V \times V$.
   531	\end{lemma}
   532	\begin{proof}
   533		A uniformly random $x \in V$ has independent components $x^{(i)}$, each uniformly distributed in $V^{(i)}$. Hence the pair $(L(x), R(x)) = \bigl( (L^{(i)}(x^{(i)}))_{i=1}^m,\, (R^{(i)}(x^{(i)}))_{i=1}^m \bigr)$ is distributed exactly as the product of the distributions $\mu_{L^{(i)},\,R^{(i)}}$ for $i = 1, 2, \dots, m$.
   534	\end{proof}

   536	\section{Typed conditionally linear distributions}
   537	% Paper section label sec:types kept for cross-reference fidelity. Only the mathematical
   538	% typed material (typed CL functions and distributions, graph distributions) is stated
   539	% here; the typed sampler and verifier machinery of the source is outside the scope of

   541	\label{sec:types}
   542	
   543	The question distribution of the Pauli basis test is \emph{typed}: each question is a pair consisting of a type, drawn together with the other player's type from the edges of a fixed \emph{type graph}, and a question content, drawn from a CL distribution determined by the pair of types.
   544	
   545	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear functions]\label{def:typed-cl-functions}
   546		\uses{def:cl-func}
   547		Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite set (the \emph{type set}) and let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$. A \emph{$\mathcal T$-typed family of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is a collection $\{L_t\}_{t \in \mathcal T}$ such that, for each $t \in \mathcal T$, $L_t$ is an $\ell$-level conditionally linear function on $V$.
   548	\end{definition}
   549	
   550	% Nonemptiness of the edge set is stated explicitly here: with E empty, m = k = 0 and the
   551	% normalization 1/(2m-k) below is undefined. The source
   552	% (references/qpbt-paper/07_types.tex:65-82) leaves this boundary hypothesis implicit.
   553	\begin{definition}[Graph distribution]\label{def:graph-distribution}
   554		Let $G = (U, E)$ be an undirected graph with vertex set $U$ and nonempty edge set $E$. Edges in $E$ are written as multisets $\{u, v\}$ of two vertices; the case $u = v$ represents a self-loop. Suppose there are $m \ge 1$ edges, $k$ of which are self-loops. Then the \emph{graph distribution $\mu_G$ of $G$} is the distribution over $U \times U$ such that for every $(u,v) \in U \times U$,
   555		\[
   556			\mu_G(u, v) =
   557			\begin{cases}
   558				1/(2m-k) & \text{if } \{u,v\} \in E\,,\\
   559				0 & \text{otherwise}\,.
   560			\end{cases}
   561		\]
   562		This is identical to the uniform distribution over ordered pairs $(u,v) \in U \times U$ such that $\{u,v\} \in E$: each edge that is not a self-loop contributes two ordered pairs, and each self-loop contributes one, whence the normalization $2m-k$.
   563	\end{definition}
   564	
   565	% The nonempty-edge hypothesis on G is inherited from def:graph-distribution, where it is
   566	% needed for the graph distribution mu_G to be defined; the source
   567	% (references/qpbt-paper/07_types.tex:84-93) leaves it implicit here as well.
   568	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear distributions]\label{def:typed-cl-distributions}
   569		\uses{def:typed-cl-functions, def:graph-distribution, def:cl-dist}
   570		Let $\mathcal T$ be a type set and let $L = \{L_u\}_{u \in \mathcal T}$ and $R = \{R_v\}_{v \in \mathcal T}$ be $\mathcal T$-typed families of conditionally linear functions on $V$. Let $G = (\mathcal T, E)$ be a graph with vertex set $\mathcal T$ and nonempty edge set $E$, so that the graph distribution $\mu_G$ of Definition~\ref{def:graph-distribution} is defined. The \emph{$(\mathcal T, G)$-typed conditionally linear distribution $\mu^G_{L,\,R}$ corresponding to $(L, R)$} is the distribution over pairs $\bigl( (u, x), (v, y) \bigr)$, where the type pair $(u,v)$ is drawn from the graph distribution $\mu_G$ and the content pair $(x,y)$ is drawn from $\mu_{L_u,\,R_v}$.

    10	\section{The classical low individual degree game}
    11	% Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    12	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    13	\label{sec:ld-game}
    14	
    15	The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.
    16	
    17	\begin{definition}[The classical low individual degree game: parameters and registers]\label{def:ld-game}
    18		\uses{def:game, def:admissible-size}
    19		% The source fixes \N to be the set of positive integers
    20		% (references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:6) and takes m, d, ldc in \N
    21		% (references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:33-35),
    22		% so the positivity below is the source's implicit domain, stated explicitly.
    23		% It is load-bearing: at d = 0 or k = 0 the prefactor a(dmk)^a of delta_ld in
    24		% lem:ld-soundness vanishes, and at d = 0 the resulting exact conclusions fail
    25		% (e.g. at (q,m,d,k) = (2,1,0,1) with eps = 1). The case k = 0, though it would
    26		% hold trivially, is likewise outside the source's domain and is omitted.
    27		The game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ is parametrized by a tuple $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$, where $m, d, k \ge 1$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}), and $m$ divides $q$. We write $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}_{\mathsf{ldparams}}$ to emphasize the dependence on the parameter tuple. The type set of $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ is
    28		\[
    29			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}} = \{\mathsf{Point}, \mathsf{ALine}, \mathsf{DLine}\}\;,
    30		\]
    31		and the distribution over type pairs $(t_{\mathrm A}, t_{\mathrm B})$ is uniform over $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}} \times \mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}}$. The ambient space is the direct sum $V = V_X \oplus V_I \oplus V_V$ of three register subspaces: the \emph{point register} $V_X \cong \F_q^m$, the \emph{coordinate register} $V_I \cong \F_q$, and the \emph{direction register} $V_V \cong \F_q^m$. Elements of $V$ are identified with triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q^m$. The question distribution and the win predicate of $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ are specified in Definitions~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} and~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} below.
    32	\end{definition}
    33	
    34	\begin{definition}[Question distribution of the classical low individual degree game]\label{def:ld-question-distribution}
    35		\uses{def:ld-game, def:cl-func, def:cl-dist, lem:cl-concat, def:cl-canonical, def:line-representative}
    36		Let $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:ld-game}. Define $L_{\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
    37		\begin{equation}
    38			\label{eq:cl-ptf}
    39			L_{\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\;.
    40		\end{equation}
    41		For $s \in \F_q$, let $\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that
    42		\begin{equation}
    43			\label{eq:chi-func}
    44			s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m} + r
    45		\end{equation}
    46		for some $0 \le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}$ under the identification of $\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}. Since $m$ divides $q$, when $s$ is uniformly distributed on $\F_q$ the index $\chi(s)$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$. Define $L_{\mathsf{ALine}}$ by
    47		\begin{equation}
    48			\label{eq:cl-alnf}
    49			L_{\mathsf{ALine}}(u,s,v) = \bigl(L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u),\, s,\, 0\bigr)\quad\text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V\;,
    50		\end{equation}
    51		where $i = \chi(s)$ and $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ denotes the canonical linear map with one-dimensional kernel spanned by $v$, used to compute canonical representatives of lines (Definition~\ref{def:line-representative}). The function $L_{\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the concatenation (in the sense of Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-concat}) of the $1$-level CL function projecting $V_I \oplus V_V$ onto $V_I$ with the family of $1$-level CL functions $\{L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}\}$ on $V_X$ indexed by $i \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$; thus $L_{\mathsf{ALine}}$ is a $2$-level CL function. Define $L_{\mathsf{DLine}}$ by
    52		\begin{equation}
    53			\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
    54			L_{\mathsf{DLine}}(u,s,v) = \bigl(L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),\, s,\, \pi_{i-1}(v)\bigr)\;,

   107	\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}
   108		The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.

   182	\section{The Magic Square game}
   183	% Paper label sec:ms kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   184	\label{sec:ms}
   185	
   186	We recall the Magic Square game of Mermin and Peres. It is a simple self-test for two EPR pairs, and it allows one to test that a pair of binary observables \emph{anticommutes}; both properties are used in the Pauli basis test. Here it is presented as a binary constraint satisfaction game. Throughout this section and the next, $\sigma^X$ and $\sigma^Z$ denote the single-qubit Pauli observables, with associated two-outcome projective measurements $\{\sigma^W_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ for $W \in \{X,Z\}$.
   187	
   188	\begin{definition}[The Magic Square game]\label{def:ms-game}
   189		\uses{def:game, def:graph-distribution}
   190		The Magic Square game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{MS}}$ is the following two-player game. There are $9$ variables $x_1,\ldots,x_9$ taking values in $\F_2$, arranged in a $3 \times 3$ grid: the cell in row $r$ and column $c$ contains the variable $x_{3(r-1)+c}$. There are $6$ linear equations over these variables: for each of the three rows and each of the first two columns, the sum of the three variables in it equals $0$; for the third column, the sum of the three variables in it equals $1$.
   191	
   192		The question types are
   193		\begin{align*}
   194			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} &= \{\mathsf{Constraint}_i : i = 1,2,\ldots,6\}\;,\\
   195			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}} &= \{\mathsf{Variable}_j : j = 1,2,\ldots,9\}\;,\\
   196			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} &= \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} \cup \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}\;,
   197		\end{align*}
   198		where $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ denotes the constraint of row $i$ (with variables $x_{3(i-1)+1}, x_{3(i-1)+2}, x_{3(i-1)+3}$), $\mathsf{Constraint}_4$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_5$ denote the constraints of the first two columns, and $\mathsf{Constraint}_6$ denotes the constraint of the third column (with variables $x_{i-3}, x_{i}, x_{i+3}$ for $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$, $i \in \{4,5,6\}$).
   199	
   200		The question distribution is as follows: the verifier samples $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ uniformly from $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$, then samples $\mathsf{Variable}_j$ uniformly among the three variables appearing in the row or column of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; one player, chosen uniformly at random, receives $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and the other receives $\mathsf{Variable}_j$. Equivalently, the verifier samples a uniformly random edge of the bipartite \emph{type graph} $G^{\mathrm{ms}}$ on vertex sets $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$ and $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}$, whose edges are $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{3(i-1)+j}$ for $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{(i-3)+3(j-1)}$ for $i \in \{4,5,6\}$, $j \in \{1,2,3\}$ ($18$ edges in total, and no self-loops), and sends one endpoint to a uniformly random player and the other endpoint to the other player.
   201	
   202		The $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player answers with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$, where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; the $\mathsf{Variable}$ player answers with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$. The players win if and only if the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player's answer satisfies the equation associated with $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   203	\end{definition}
   204	
   205	The following theorem records the self-testing (rigidity) properties of the Magic Square game. It is used in the soundness analysis of the Pauli basis test to enforce anticommutation relations between certain pairs of observables.
   206	
   207	\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]\label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   208		\uses{def:ms-game, def:tensor-product-value, def:EPR, def:povm-distance}
   209		Let $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{MS}}$ with probability $1-\eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \hilb_{\mathrm A} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B}$. Then there exist local isometries $\phi_{\mathrm A}\colon \hilb_{\mathrm A} \to \hilb_{\mathrm A'} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm A''}$ and $\phi_{\mathrm B}\colon \hilb_{\mathrm B} \to \hilb_{\mathrm B'} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$, where $\hilb_{\mathrm A'}, \hilb_{\mathrm B'} \cong (\C^2)^{\ot 2}$ and $\hilb_{\mathrm A''}, \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$ are finite dimensional, and a state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}} \in \hilb_{\mathrm A''} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$, such that:
   210		\begin{enumerate}
   211			\item $\bigl\| \phi_{\mathrm A} \ot \phi_{\mathrm B} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot 2} \ot \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \bigr\| \le O(\sqrt\eps)$;
   212			\item letting $\tilde A^x_a = \phi_{\mathrm A} A^x_a \phi_{\mathrm A}^\dagger$ and $\tilde B^y_b = \phi_{\mathrm B} B^y_b \phi_{\mathrm B}^\dagger$,
   213			\begin{align*}
   214				\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_b \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} (\sigma^X_b)_{\mathrm A'} \ot I_{\mathrm{A''B'B''}}\;,\\
   215				\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_b \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} (\sigma^Z_b)_{\mathrm A'} \ot I_{\mathrm{A''B'B''}}\;,\\
   260		so the bottom-right cell is Hermitian, and it squares to the identity; hence every cell is a genuine $\pm 1$-valued observable. The three observables in each row and each column commute pairwise --- for the third row and third column this again uses Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian} --- so the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ measurements are well defined, and the strategy is symmetric, projective, and commuting. A two-outcome projective measurement is consistent on a state if and only if its observable $\mathcal O$ satisfies $\mathcal O \ot I \ket{\psi} = I \ot \mathcal O \ket{\psi}$; since $A$ and $B$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot n}$ by hypothesis and $\sigma^X$, $\sigma^Z$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$, each cell observable is a product of consistent, commuting factors and is therefore consistent on $\ket{\psi}$, and consistency of the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ measurements follows from the cellwise consistencies together with commutativity. Finally, the observables in each row and each of the first two columns multiply to $I$, while those of the third column multiply to $-I$; for the measurement $\{S_0, S_1\}$ obtained by measuring a $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ triple and outputting the sum of the three bits, the observable $S_0 - S_1$ equals the product of the three cell observables, hence $\pm I$, which forces the three answer bits to sum to $0$ (respectively, $1$ for $\mathsf{Constraint}_6$) with certainty. Together with consistency this shows that every check of the Magic Square game is passed with probability $1$, so the strategy has value $1$.
   261	\end{proof}

   263	\section{The Pauli basis test}
   264	% Paper label sec:qld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   265	\label{sec:qld-game}
   266	
   267	The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

   501		\begin{enumerate}

 \section{Distance measures}
 
 \begin{definition}[Distance between states]\label{def:state-distance}
 	Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ be two families of states in the same space $\mathcal H$. For a function $\delta \colon \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted $\ket{\psi} \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if
 	\[
 		\lVert \ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n} \rVert^2 = O(\delta(n))\,.
 	\]
 	The dependence of the states and of $\delta$ on the indexing parameter $n$ is generally left implicit; we write, e.g., $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.
 \end{definition}
 
 \begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]\label{def:consistency}
 	\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.consistencyDefect, MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsConsistentWithin}
 	\leanok
 	\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
 	Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ be POVMs. We write
 	\[
 		A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a
 	\]
 	on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
 	\[
 		\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi} = O(\delta)\,.
 	\]
 	In this case we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$. As in Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}, the $O(\cdot)$ refers to families of POVMs and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and is taken as $n \to \infty$.
 \end{definition}
 
 A measurement that is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same state under the singleton distribution, and vice versa: if $\sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = 1$, then $M_a \ot \Id\, \ket{\psi} = \Id \ot M_a\, \ket{\psi}$ for every $a$, by the equality case of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied outcome by outcome.

 	\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
 	Let $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal A$ be finite sets and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
 	\[
 		\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_a \lVert (M^x_a - N^x_a)\, \ket{\psi} \rVert^2 \le O(\delta)\,,
 	\]

 theorem for the Pauli basis test, Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}, stated in
 Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}. Starting from a strategy that succeeds in the

 are used to define a set of observables that correspond to a subset of the
 Pauli $X$ and $Z$ observables, and these observables are shown to
 approximately satisfy the associated Pauli group relations. In
 Section~\ref{sec:expanding}, ancillary registers containing EPR states are
 adjoined to the players' state, and a new set of approximately commuting
 observables acting on the expanded state is defined.
 Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} combines the approximately commuting
 observables into a strategy for the \emph{classical} low individual degree
 test and applies the soundness theorem of that test to construct a single
 projective measurement that simultaneously measures all of them.
 Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} uses this simultaneous measurement to
 construct an exact representation of the Pauli group, shows that it is close
 to the original strategy observables on the expanded state, and deduces
 Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}. Section~\ref{sec:qld-prelim} below collects
 preliminary definitions and lemmas used throughout the analysis.

 players' state and lifts the strategy observables and measurements to the
 expanded state. The point of the construction is that the ancilla factor of

 Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. Instead, the construction relies on the low \emph{individual} degree test, whose quantum soundness is proved in~\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} and generalized in~\cite{Ji2021Quantum}. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.

 \section{The Magic Square game}
 % Paper label sec:ms kept for cross-reference fidelity.
 \label{sec:ms}
 
 We recall the Magic Square game of Mermin and Peres. It is a simple self-test for two EPR pairs, and it allows one to test that a pair of binary observables \emph{anticommutes}; both properties are used in the Pauli basis test. Here it is presented as a binary constraint satisfaction game. Throughout this section and the next, $\sigma^X$ and $\sigma^Z$ denote the single-qubit Pauli observables, with associated two-outcome projective measurements $\{\sigma^W_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ for $W \in \{X,Z\}$.
 
 \begin{definition}[The Magic Square game]\label{def:ms-game}
 	\uses{def:game, def:graph-distribution}
 	The Magic Square game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{MS}}$ is the following two-player game. There are $9$ variables $x_1,\ldots,x_9$ taking values in $\F_2$, arranged in a $3 \times 3$ grid: the cell in row $r$ and column $c$ contains the variable $x_{3(r-1)+c}$. There are $6$ linear equations over these variables: for each of the three rows and each of the first two columns, the sum of the three variables in it equals $0$; for the third column, the sum of the three variables in it equals $1$.
 
 	The question types are
 	\begin{align*}
 		\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} &= \{\mathsf{Constraint}_i : i = 1,2,\ldots,6\}\;,\\
 		\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}} &= \{\mathsf{Variable}_j : j = 1,2,\ldots,9\}\;,\\
 		\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} &= \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} \cup \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}\;,
 	\end{align*}
 	where $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ denotes the constraint of row $i$ (with variables $x_{3(i-1)+1}, x_{3(i-1)+2}, x_{3(i-1)+3}$), $\mathsf{Constraint}_4$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_5$ denote the constraints of the first two columns, and $\mathsf{Constraint}_6$ denotes the constraint of the third column (with variables $x_{i-3}, x_{i}, x_{i+3}$ for $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$, $i \in \{4,5,6\}$).
 
 	The question distribution is as follows: the verifier samples $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ uniformly from $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$, then samples $\mathsf{Variable}_j$ uniformly among the three variables appearing in the row or column of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; one player, chosen uniformly at random, receives $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and the other receives $\mathsf{Variable}_j$. Equivalently, the verifier samples a uniformly random edge of the bipartite \emph{type graph} $G^{\mathrm{ms}}$ on vertex sets $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$ and $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}$, whose edges are $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{3(i-1)+j}$ for $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{(i-3)+3(j-1)}$ for $i \in \{4,5,6\}$, $j \in \{1,2,3\}$ ($18$ edges in total, and no self-loops), and sends one endpoint to a uniformly random player and the other endpoint to the other player.
 
 	The $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player answers with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$, where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; the $\mathsf{Variable}$ player answers with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$. The players win if and only if the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player's answer satisfies the equation associated with $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
 \end{definition}
 
 The following theorem records the self-testing (rigidity) properties of the Magic Square game. It is used in the soundness analysis of the Pauli basis test to enforce anticommutation relations between certain pairs of observables.

 \begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]\label{thm:ms-rigidity}
 	\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.exists_ms_rigidity}
 	\leanok
 	\uses{def:ms-game, def:tensor-product-value, def:EPR, def:povm-distance}
 	Let $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{MS}}$ with probability $1-\eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \hilb_{\mathrm A} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B}$. Then there exist local isometries $\phi_{\mathrm A}\colon \hilb_{\mathrm A} \to \hilb_{\mathrm A'} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm A''}$ and $\phi_{\mathrm B}\colon \hilb_{\mathrm B} \to \hilb_{\mathrm B'} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$, where $\hilb_{\mathrm A'}, \hilb_{\mathrm B'} \cong (\C^2)^{\ot 2}$ and $\hilb_{\mathrm A''}, \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$ are finite dimensional, and a state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}} \in \hilb_{\mathrm A''} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$, such that:
 	\begin{enumerate}
 		\item $\bigl\| \phi_{\mathrm A} \ot \phi_{\mathrm B} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot 2} \ot \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \bigr\| \le O(\sqrt\eps)$;
 		\item letting $\tilde A^x_a = \phi_{\mathrm A} A^x_a \phi_{\mathrm A}^\dagger$ and $\tilde B^y_b = \phi_{\mathrm B} B^y_b \phi_{\mathrm B}^\dagger$,
 		\begin{align*}
 			\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_b \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} (\sigma^X_b)_{\mathrm A'} \ot I_{\mathrm{A''B'B''}}\;,\\
 			\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_b \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} (\sigma^Z_b)_{\mathrm A'} \ot I_{\mathrm{A''B'B''}}\;,\\
 			I_{\mathrm{A'A''}} \ot \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_b &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} I_{\mathrm{A'A''B''}} \ot (\sigma^X_b)_{\mathrm B'}\;,\\
 			I_{\mathrm{A'A''}} \ot \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_b &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} I_{\mathrm{A'A''B''}} \ot (\sigma^Z_b)_{\mathrm B'}\;,
 		\end{align*}
 		where each $\approx_{\sqrt\eps}$ holds with respect to the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot 2}_{\mathrm{A'B'}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{aux}}_{\mathrm{A''B''}}$ and the answer summation is over $b \in \{0,1\}$, and the approximation bounds carry implicit universal constants.
 	\end{enumerate}
 	As a consequence, letting $\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1} = \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_0 - \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_1$ and $\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} = \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_0 - \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_1$ denote the associated observables, it holds that
 	\begin{align*}
 		\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1} \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} -\, \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1} \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}}\;,\\
 		I_{\mathrm{A'A''}} \ot \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_1} \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} -\, I_{\mathrm{A'A''}} \ot \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}\;,
 	\end{align*}
 	where, for operators $M$, $N$ that are not POVM elements, the notation $M \approx_\delta N$ means $\bra{\psi} (M-N)^\dagger (M-N) \ket{\psi} \le O(\delta)$ with respect to the same state.
 \end{theorem}
 \begin{proof}
 	This result is imported from Theorem~6.9 of~\cite{Coladangelo2017Robust}. There are two minor differences between their statement and the one given here. First, they state a robustness of $O(\eps)$, but measure the closeness of the actual and ideal states in trace norm; expressed as the Euclidean distance between $\phi_{\mathrm A} \ot \phi_{\mathrm B}\ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot 2} \ot \ket{\mathrm{aux}}$, this becomes $O(\sqrt\eps)$. Second, their ideal observables for the $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_5$ questions are $I \ot \sigma^Z$ and $\sigma^Z\sigma^X \ot \sigma^Z\sigma^X$; under a local change of basis these are equivalent to $\sigma^X \ot I$ and $\sigma^Z \ot I$, respectively.
 \end{proof}
 
 The converse construction shows that any pair of anticommuting binary observables yields a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game.

   459	
   460	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of

   463	
   464	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   465		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   466		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   467		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   468			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   469		\end{equation}
   470		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   471		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   472		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   473		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   474		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   475		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   476		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   477		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   478	\end{definition}
   479	
   480	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   481		\uses{def:line}
   482		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   483		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   484	\end{proposition}
   485	\begin{proof}
   486		\uses{def:line}
   487		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   488		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   489		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   490		inclusion.
   491	\end{proof}
   492	
   493	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   494	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   495	representation is obtained as follows.

   501		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$

   503		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   504		\[
   505			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   506		\]
   507		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   508		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with

 \begin{remark}[Two steps in the source proof of the extraction lemma]\label{rem:qld-unitary-triangle-slip}
 	In the source proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary}, the triangle inequality gives $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \| \leq \| (\Id - H_X)\ket{\vartheta} \| + \| (\Id - H_Z)\ket{\vartheta} \| \leq 2\sqrt{\delta_S}$, so that $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \leq 4\delta_S$; the source instead asserts the bound $2\sqrt{\delta_S}$ for the \emph{squared} norm, which holds only when $\sqrt{\delta_S} \leq 1/2$, and consequently carries the term $\sqrt{\delta_S}$ into an overlap bound of $1 - 2\delta_S - \sqrt{\delta_S}$. The proof above uses the corrected bound $4\delta_S$, which gives the overlap bound $1 - 4\delta_S$ and leaves the final bound $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}} = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$ unchanged. The source proof also normalizes the vector $(\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\vartheta}$ without ensuring that it is nonzero; the case distinction on $\delta_S$ in the proof above supplies this, the conclusions of the lemma being trivial when $\delta_S$ exceeds a universal constant.
 \end{remark}

 % lines 1415--1877 (subsection ``Pulling the X and Z measurements apart''
 % and the closing proof of the soundness theorem).
 
 This chapter completes the analysis of the Pauli basis test~\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple (Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), $q = 2^t$, and $M = 2^m$ denotes the number of $q$-ary qudits tested for per player. (The letter $M$ also denotes measurement operators, always carrying super- and subscripts; the meaning is determined by context, as in the source.)
